entries.clue: Cheers when multinational acquires USA resort (8)

indicatorNotes.acquires: the company takes the other letters into itself
indicatorNotes.resort: to re-sort USA is to put its letters in a new order

annotation.surface: A tech giant buys up an American holiday destination, and somebody raises a glass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resort' reads as a noun, a holiday spot; it is the verb re-sort.
annotation.definitionFit: Applause is the cheering of an approving crowd.

entries.clue: Check car presented by Treasury head (5)

indicatorNotes.head: the head of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A car is handed over by the man in charge of the Treasury, perhaps as a perk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Treasury head' looks like the Chancellor; it is only the letter T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an inspection of the books is a check on them, and the verb works the same way.

entries.clue: Maybe Andrew welcomes island power with liberal rule? (9)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: the prince takes the other letters in, as a host welcomes guests

blocks.note: Andrew is one example of a prince, hence 'maybe'

annotation.surface: A satirical jab at the disgraced Prince Andrew enjoying an island getaway and a very relaxed set of rules.
annotation.walkthrough: IPL goes inside PRINC…E. The question mark covers 'Maybe Andrew' as an example of a prince.
annotation.definitionFit: A principle is a rule of conduct or a governing law.

entries.clue: A New York institution for no one in particular (7)

blocks.note: a body is an institution or organisation

annotation.surface: A New York organisation that exists to serve nobody in particular.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Institution' looks like a college or museum; it is only a body, and the surface's New York organisation sets up the joke that it serves nobody special.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Anybody' refers to any person at all, no one in particular.

entries.clue: Treasury's coffers somewhat depleted – gulp! (5)

indicatorNotes.somewhat depleted: only part of the phrase is kept, the rest used up

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

annotation.surface: A gasp of alarm at how empty the national coffers have become.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gulp' looks like a nervous exclamation; it is the verb, to eat greedily. To scoff food is to wolf it down.
annotation.definitionFit: To scoff is to gulp down food greedily.

entries.clue: Retiring pensioner welcoming sex in paved area (5)

indicatorNotes.Retiring: going backwards, as one retires or withdraws
indicatorNotes.welcoming: the pensioner takes the other letters in

blocks.note: 'it' is a coy word for sex, placed inside O…AP to make OITAP

annotation.surface: A newly retired pensioner getting frisky out on the paving stones.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' looks like the pensioner giving up work; it turns OITAP round.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: the flagged terrace outside the back door is exactly a paved area.

entries.clue: Deal in drugs before sick leave (4,3)

blocks.note: to push drugs is to sell them

annotation.surface: A worker dealing drugs just before calling in sick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sick leave' reads as one phrase; the definition is 'leave' alone.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: pushing a boat away from the bank became slang for going away.

entries.clue: Energy hoarded by that bastard character (5)

indicatorNotes.hoarded by: the E is kept inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.bastard: THAT is corrupted, its letters debased into a new order

annotation.surface: Some lout is hogging all the energy, and the speaker is furious about his character.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as a person's nature; it is a letter of an alphabet, here Greek.
annotation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: Eton, for many a peer getting on coach (3,6)

blocks.note: to school someone is to coach them

annotation.surface: An ageing lord climbing aboard a coach, with a dig at Eton's grip on the peerage.
annotation.walkthrough: Eton is the famous English private school that has educated many lords, so it is 'the old school' to them.
annotation.definitionFit: One's old school is where one was educated, and Eton is that for many peers.

entries.clue: Unstable person taking drugs, making comeback (8)

indicatorNotes.Unstable: PERSON is not steady, so its letters shift
indicatorNotes.taking: the rearranged letters take in the drugs

blocks.note: E = ecstasy, so ES are drugs, placed after the R

annotation.surface: A troubled addict staging a return to public life.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Comeback' looks like a return to fame; it is a retort.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of a retort, the reply that comes back at a remark.

entries.clue: (&21dn.) Living provided by Mail? Second-class, awfully dear (5)

indicatorNotes.awfully: DEAR is treated badly, its letters jumbled

blocks.note: the Mail is a Daily, a daily paper

annotation.surface: A dig at the Daily Mail as a second-rate paper that costs too much.
annotation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British tabloid newspaper, so a 'Mail' is a daily. The question mark flags that example.
annotation.definitionFit: One's daily bread is one's livelihood, a living.

entries.clue: Pay too much for some lover's pendant (9)

indicatorNotes.some: only some of the letters are used

annotation.surface: Someone overpays for a piece of jewellery to give their lover.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's pricey pendant is itself a case of paying too much, so the definition slots neatly into the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spending beyond what is right is paying too much.

entries.clue: Give a bollocking to Mark (4,3)

blocks.note: a phrasal verb meaning to scold
a verb: to put a check mark against an item on a list

annotation.surface: Somebody named Mark is about to get a severe telling-off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mark' is capitalised to look like a man's name; it is the verb. A bollocking is British slang for a severe scolding.
annotation.definitionFit: Tick off means both to scold someone and to mark an item as done.

entries.clue: Mundane reasons for overturning US agency (7)

indicatorNotes.overturning: the letters are turned over, end to end

blocks.note: pros = reasons for, as in pros and cons
CIA, the US intelligence agency, turned round

annotation.surface: A dull justification offered for abolishing an American government agency.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'reasons for overturning' as one phrase; 'for' belongs to PROS, and 'overturning' acts on the agency.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: writing like prose rather than poetry came to mean ordinary, mundane.

entries.clue: Be very critical about gutless party's childish habit (5)

indicatorNotes.about: to turn about is to face the other way, so the word is read backwards
indicatorNotes.gutless: the party's insides are removed, leaving its outside letters

blocks.note: to pan is to criticise harshly; PAN turned round

annotation.surface: Attacking a spineless political party for its infantile behaviour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Habit' looks like a behaviour; it is clothing, as a nun's habit is. A nappy is the British word for a diaper.
annotation.definitionFit: A nappy is what a baby wears, so a child's garment or habit.

entries.clue: Peter Pan's bollocks, containing nothing that would be of use to a writer (9)

annotation.definition: that would be of use to a writer
annotation.definitionNote: a relative clause standing for 'something that would be of use to a writer'

indicatorNotes.bollocks: slang for rubbish, so PETER PAN is turned into nonsense
indicatorNotes.containing: the jumbled letters hold the O

blocks.note: O = nothing, zero, placed after the N

annotation.surface: A rude dismissal of Peter Pan as useless material for any author.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks' is British slang for nonsense, here telling you to scramble the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description rather than a synonym: sheets for letters are the stock-in-trade of anyone who writes.

entries.clue: Ex-world leader covers up finest broken political promises (9)

annotation.definitionNote: plural phrase for a single document listing them

indicatorNotes.covers up: MAO goes around the other letters
indicatorNotes.broken: FINEST is broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: Mao Zedong, former leader of China

annotation.surface: A former head of state hiding the fact that the best political promises have been broken.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broken political promises' reads as one cynical phrase; 'broken' belongs to FINEST.
annotation.definitionFit: A manifesto is a party's published set of political promises.

entries.clue: Ann Widdecombe finally in the shit, spiteful thing (8)

annotation.definitionNote: noun phrase for an abstract noun; meanness here is a spiteful act

indicatorNotes.in: ANN and E go inside the mess

annotation.surface: Ann Widdecombe, the outspoken Conservative politician, finally landing in trouble over something nasty.
annotation.walkthrough: Ann Widdecombe is a British ex-Tory MP. Her name splits: ANN is taken whole, Widdecombe gives only E.
annotation.definitionFit: The abstract noun used for a single instance: an unkind act can be called by the quality it shows.

entries.clue: Plot involving Sun and Conservative way of doing things (9)

blocks.note: a line, as in the party line, is a way of doing things

annotation.surface: A conspiracy linking the Sun newspaper and the Conservative Party's methods.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sun' looks like the British tabloid; it is just S.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the line a narrative follows is its plot.

entries.clue: Neat, these bent politicians – Republicans mainly now (3,6)

indicatorNotes.bent: the letters are bent out of shape

annotation.surface: A jibe at crooked politicians, now mostly Republican.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bent' is British slang for corrupt, which suits politicians, but here it scrambles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The US Senate is a body of politicians, currently with a Republican majority.

entries.clue: Just once, behave extremely lousily (7)

indicatorNotes.extremely: only the extremes, the first and last letters

annotation.surface: A plea: behave appallingly just this once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Just once' reads as a phrase, but 'Just' is the definition, in its sense of precisely.
annotation.definitionFit: Just and exactly both mean precisely.

entries.clue: Lord Owen's initial drunken drivel (5)

indicatorNotes.initial: just the first letter of Owen
indicatorNotes.drunken: the letters stagger into a new order

annotation.surface: A peer, Lord Owen, whose opening speech was drunken nonsense.
annotation.walkthrough: Lord Owen is David Owen, the former British Foreign Secretary; 'initial' takes only his O.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean dribbling saliva and, figuratively, foolish talk.

entries.clue: Dreary Adolf, not one to get involved with EU left (7)

annotation.surface: A gloomy Adolf refusing to have anything to do with the left-wing European Union.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Adolf' tempts you to think of Hitler, but only its letters matter once the A for 'one' is gone.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: full of dole, an old word for grief, so gloomy and dreary.

entries.clue: Apply drug at right time when in agony? (7)

indicatorNotes.in: 'when in agony' puts the drug-right-time letters inside the word for agony

annotation.surface: Advice on taking a painkiller at the proper moment when the pain comes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Apply' looks like applying a treatment; it means to be relevant.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of being relevant, as a rule applies to a case.

entries.clue: A place to sleep or maybe love, by the way (5)

indicatorNotes.maybe: OR could be another arrangement of its letters

annotation.surface: A bed, or perhaps love by the roadside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' looks like it offers love as an alternative; it jumbles OR.
annotation.definitionFit: A roost is where birds settle to sleep.

entries.clue: Bishop rigged pulley to attain female missionary position (5,2)

indicatorNotes.rigged: the pulley is set up differently

annotation.surface: A bishop sets up a hoist to reach a certain sexual position, a dig at clerical hypocrisy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Missionary position' is the sex position with the woman on her back, which is belly up for her.
annotation.definitionFit: Belly up means lying on one's back, as the woman does in the missionary position.

entries.clue: see 9ac. (5)
Strokes bottom of Tory scapegoat (5)

indicatorNotes.bottom of: in a down entry the bottom is the last letter

annotation.surface: Someone fondling a Conservative's backside, then blaming another.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' invites a rude reading; it is the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A patsy is someone set up to take the blame, a scapegoat.

entries.clue: Unseemly, shit Republican gets smack (4,5)

annotation.definitionNote: adjective for a noun phrase, as in 'in poor taste'

blocks.note: a smack is a taste or flavour, as in a smack of garlic

annotation.surface: A crude Republican politician gets a slap for bad behaviour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a blow or heroin; it is a hint of flavour.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom standing for an adjective: an unseemly joke is said to be in bad taste.

entries.clue: One who chats up Reform leader in broken-down lift (5)

indicatorNotes.leader: only the first letter of Reform
indicatorNotes.in: R goes inside the rearranged lift

annotation.surface: A Reform UK party leader using a stuck lift to make advances on someone.
annotation.walkthrough: Reform UK is a British right-wing party; its 'leader' here is just R.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a person given to playful romantic advances is one who chats others up.

entries.clue: Democrat-type houses cross (5)

indicatorNotes.houses: the phrase holds the answer inside it

annotation.surface: A Democratic type of house, as if homes had party affiliations.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a noun or verb; it is the adjective, angry.
annotation.definitionFit: Ratty is British informal for irritable, cross.

entries.clue: Mature blend of rye? That's cheating (8)

indicatorNotes.blend of: the letters of RYE are mixed

annotation.surface: A whisky taster wonders if a mature rye blend is a con.
annotation.walkthrough: The whisky picture (mature, blend, rye) hides a marital betrayal.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific sense of the definition: cheating on a spouse by sleeping with someone else.
